The incubation period of the Marabou stork begins once the clutch is complete, with eggs maintained by the attending adults at a stable temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Hatching occurs after an incubation period of approximately 30 days [ab = approximately 30 days], a duration typical for a large ciconiiform bird at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. At the moment of hatching, the altricial nestlings emerge with a wet weight at birth of 68 grams [Wwb = 68 grams], reflecting the considerable yolk reserves invested by the female. This initial mass is modest relative to the ultimate adult size the chick will attain, necessitating a prolonged period of intensive biparental provisioning. The downy chicks are brooded continuously during their first week to maintain thermoregulatory stability, as their own endothermic capacity develops slowly. The timing of hatching in wild populations is often synchronized with seasonal flood pulses that concentrate fish and amphibian prey, ensuring a reliable food supply for the rapidly growing broods.

Under the warm thermal conditions of the African savanna, typically recorded at 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], the nestlings pass through several critical developmental milestones. The age at fledging, when young birds achieve their first sustained flight, occurs at approximately 100 days after hatching [tx = approximately 100 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This relatively prolonged nestling period is characteristic of large wading birds and allows for the complete development of the flight feathers and the musculature necessary for soaring flight. Before fledging, the chicks undergo a rapid phase of somatic growth, transitioning from a downy covering to juvenile plumage. Parental attendance remains high throughout this period, with both adults delivering regurgitated food to the nest multiple times daily. Mortality during the nestling stage can be substantial, particularly during droughts when parents may struggle to locate sufficient prey, leading to sibling competition and, occasionally, obligate siblicide among younger chicks.

Sexual maturation in the Marabou stork is not achieved rapidly despite its large body size. Puberty, defined as the attainment of gonadal maturity, occurs at approximately 300 days after hatching [tp = approximately 300 days after hatching] under the prevailing ambient conditions of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. However, behavioral and physiological readiness for breeding does not immediately follow; young birds often spend an extended period as non-breeding floaters before securing a territory. The maximum reproductive rate for this species, reported as approximately 2 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 2 offspring per year], has been documented under optimal foraging conditions and at the same thermal regime. Breeding pairs typically produce a single clutch per year, laying 1 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 to 3 eggs per clutch] per annum [F_R_i = per annum]. This low fecundity is compensated by high parental investment in each offspring and a relatively low adult mortality rate. The reproductive output is strongly influenced by local prey abundance, with birds in resource-rich wetlands achieving higher fledging success than those in more marginal habitats.

The first successful brood for a Marabou stork is typically deferred well beyond the point of initial sexual maturity, reflecting the challenges of territory acquisition and pair formation. The time since birth at first brood is 1460 days [tR = 1460 days], recorded under the species' typical active body temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This protracted delay before first reproduction is a common life-history strategy among large, long-lived birds, allowing individuals to gain foraging experience and establish a stable nesting site. Females and males attain significantly different ultimate sizes, a fact reflected in their maximum adult body masses. The ultimate wet weight for females reaches 7000 grams [Wwi = 7000 grams], while males are considerably heavier, attaining an ultimate wet weight of 8500 grams [Wwi = 8500 grams]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism is among the most extreme within the Ciconiidae and is thought to relate to male-male competition for nest sites and the need for males to defend territories effectively.

The maximum lifespan recorded for the Marabou stork is considerable, reflecting the species' position as a slow-living, K-selected strategist. In wild populations, the oldest confirmed individuals attain a lifespan of approximately 44.7 years [am = approximately 44.7 years], though this estimate is derived from birds living under the typical thermal conditions of their sub-Saharan range, near 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This remarkable longevity is supported by a scavenging and predatory diet that buffers against extreme food shortages, as carrion and human refuse provide a relatively stable resource base throughout the year. Older birds often exhibit a predictable pattern of reproductive senescence, with clutch sizes and fledging success declining in the final years of life. The species also exhibits a notable tolerance for high ambient temperatures, facilitated by behaviors such as urohidrosis—the defecation on the legs—which provides evaporative cooling. This thermoregulatory adaptation is particularly valuable for a large, dark-plumaged bird foraging in open landscapes under intense solar radiation.
